newsitem.title: USA: US T-bond eyes post-correction 6.75-pct anchor.
newsitem.headline: US T-bond eyes post-correction 6.75-pct anchor.

text.p: The U.S. 30-year Treasury bond, though vulnerable to year-end selling pressure, can count on solid buying interest at a 6.75-percent yield, experts said.

"Nothing is likely to occur on the fundamental economic side any time in the near future to tell us what the appropriate yield is. Bonds will drift around," predicted Charles Lieberman, managing director at Chase Securities.
"But everyone and their uncle will buy at 6.75 percent. That's the next level where people will find support for the market," Lieberman said.
Following the November U.S. presidential elections, Treasuries embarked on a rally that brought the yield on the 30-year bond down from the 6-3/4-percent area to a low of 6.36 percent on December 2.

But Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's December 5 words of caution about asset overvaluation resulted in a sharp selloff in U.S. equities and debt -- bringing the bond yield back up to 6.62 percent at the close on Thursday.

Three chief economists -- William Dudley at Goldman, Sachs and Co., Stuart Hoffman at PNC Bank, and David Resler at Nomura Securities International -- agreed bonds will attract buyers at 6.75 percent, though their rationales differ.

Dudley, whose firm, Goldman Sachs, recommended shorting bonds at 6.35 percent, contended that "at 6.75 percent, you have to say it's a reasonable place to start buying," given the outlook for a steady Fed policy.
"A lot of the optimism that was in the market was washed away," Dudley said, referring to the recent market selloff in the wake of Greenspan's speech.
"Before, the market was thinking an easing was more likely than a tightening for the Fed's next move. Now, it's deemed by bulls and bears alike as no change of monetary policy stance," he added.
Dudley expected fresh selling pressure until bond yields reached 6.75 percent on anticipation of strong economic numbers.
Resler, at Nomura, declared "himself prepared to be a buyer of bonds at 6.75 percent" because the market no longer needs to price in the political or inflation risks perceived through early November.

"We broke out of the 6.50/7.0-percent range after the elections produced a result the market liked. Meanwhile, the economic fundamentals changed quite a bit and that's what put us in that lower range," Resler explained. "I see no reason why we should climb back into that (6.50/7.0-percent) range."
The Nomura economist attributed the recent Treasury selloff in part to the lack of a customary coupon pass by the Fed and to year-end book-squaring.
Hoffman at PNC pointed out that the rally/selloff sequence has restored a two-way market -- meaning there are bargain-hunters ready to step in for value.
"Persistent selling days in and days out are unlikely because it is a two-way market. Fundamental buyers would materialize if we are back at 6.75 percent," Hoffman predicted.
Hoffman said Greenspan's speech had brought the market back to a more balanced evaluation of risks.
"With the two-year note sitting under 5.60 percent, people were beginning to believe the Fed might actually lower rates early next year," Hoffman said.
"Now, the market is priced for a more neutral view. The next Fed move is a toss-up, without any reason to go one way or another." Hoffman added.

J.P. Morgan senior economist Marc Wanshel agreed. "The market went ahead of itself (in the recent rally) but the correction is done," he said. "We are not far away from realistic valuation. We have seen most of the volatility."

Wanshel expected the long bond yield to hover in "a 6.40- to 6.80-percent range, likely in the upper end of the range" in part because foreign investors are less aggressive in their buying of U.S. debt.
"The buying by foreigners based on the currencies play, using very low-cost funding overseas to buy U.S. assets -- this trade had to come to an end," Wanshel said.
